title: European Stroke Organisation and European Academy of Neurology joint guidelines on post-stroke cognitive impairment
shortTitle: European Stroke Organisation and European Academy of Neurology joint

recommendations.text: Evidence does not support recommending monitored lifestyle changes solely to prevent cognitive decline or dementia after stroke; this assessment concerns cognitive outcomes only.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 1; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: Do not use lifestyle interventions alone or in combination solely to prevent post-stroke cognitive decline or dementia. Physical and mental health benefits and prevention of cardiovascular disease may still justify them. Adequately powered trials of their cognitive effects after stroke are needed.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 1; consensus 1

recommendations.section: PICO 2: Intensive blood pressure treatment and cognition
recommendations.text: No recommendation can be made for intensive rather than usual blood pressure treatment solely to prevent post-stroke cognitive decline or dementia. This does not address its vascular benefits.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 2; recommendation 1

recommendations.section: PICO 2: Dual antiplatelets and cognition in lacunar stroke
recommendations.text: For prevention of cognitive decline after lacunar stroke, dual antiplatelet therapy is discouraged compared with a single antiplatelet. This recommendation is limited to cognitive effects in lacunar stroke.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 2; recommendation 2

recommendations.text: No recommendation can be made for intensive rather than usual statin treatment solely to prevent post-stroke cognitive decline or dementia; other indications are outside this cognitive-outcome assessment.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 2; recommendation 3

recommendations.section: PICO 2: Vascular prevention despite uncertain cognitive benefit
recommendations.text: Continue comprehensive vascular prevention after stroke, including blood pressure treatment, antithrombotics and statins, because recurrent stroke and cardiovascular benefits remain relevant despite uncertain cognitive benefit. Risk-factor targets evolve; previously intensive regimens may now be standard. Include cognitive outcomes in future secondary-prevention trials.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 2; consensus 1

recommendations.text: No recommendation can be made for combined medication and lifestyle programmes solely to prevent post-stroke cognitive decline or dementia.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 3; recommendation 1

recommendations.section: PICO 3: Multicomponent prevention and other benefits
recommendations.text: All but one writing-group member agreed that monitored multicomponent programmes cannot be recommended for cognitive prevention alone, while their potential to prevent recurrent stroke or cardiovascular disease remains relevant.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 3; consensus 1

recommendations.text: The benefits and limitations of cognitive training for preventing cognitive decline or dementia after stroke remain uncertain.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 4; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: All but one writing-group member supported considering cognitive training within a broader rehabilitation programme. Cognitive training by itself has no demonstrated clinically meaningful or sustained preventive effect on post-stroke cognitive decline or dementia.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 4; consensus 1

recommendations.text: In post-stroke dementia, the cognitive and quality-of-life benefits and risks of continuing versus withdrawing antihypertensives or statins remain uncertain.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 5; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: Continue pharmacological vascular risk management in mild-to-moderate post-stroke dementia, given vascular benefit and no clear cognitive harm signal. In advanced dementia with short life expectancy, harms and treatment burden may outweigh vascular protection, so benefit is unclear. Pragmatic deprescribing trials are needed in advanced post-stroke dementia.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 5; consensus 1

recommendations.text: Trials do not establish whether routine screening of every stroke patient improves stroke care. This uncertainty applies to universal screening, not clinician-directed cognitive assessment.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 6; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: Consider cognitive screening within comprehensive assessment of stroke survivors. Evidence does not establish optimal timing, content or benefit to patients, carers or health systems. Future studies should include acute care, feasibility and acceptability, care pathways, carer outcomes and health economics.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 6; consensus 1

recommendations.text: Consider MoCA screening in post-acute stroke, without substituting it for comprehensive clinical assessment. Conventional cut-offs identify most important cognitive problems but produce many false positives; consider a lower threshold in stroke populations.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 7; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: MoCA relies on visuospatial and language abilities. Its initial screening performance is acceptable, but more accessible tools are needed for communication problems or neglect. Use trained examiners; a positive result warrants comprehensive cognitive assessment and sharing findings with the stroke team.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 7; consensus 1

recommendations.text: Consider MMSE screening in acute or post-acute stroke, without replacing comprehensive clinical assessment. Conventional cut-offs exclude most people without important cognitive problems but miss a substantial number who do have them.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 8; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: MMSE depends on visuospatial and language abilities. Although acceptable for initial screening, more feasible tools are needed for communication difficulties or neglect. Examiners should be trained; positive screens require comprehensive cognitive assessment with results shared with the stroke team.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 8; consensus 1

recommendations.text: An ACE version may be considered for cognitive screening in acute or post-acute stroke, alongside rather than instead of comprehensive clinical assessment. Performance varies with the positivity threshold; evidence does not identify an optimal stroke cut-off.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 9; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: ACE versions require visuospatial and language abilities, and acceptable initial screening properties in stroke have not been established. Develop more feasible tools for communication impairment or neglect. Use trained examiners; follow a positive ACE with comprehensive cognitive assessment and communicate findings to the stroke team.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 9; consensus 1

recommendations.section: PICO 10: Oxford Cognitive Screen diagnostic accuracy
recommendations.text: Published evidence is insufficient to determine OCS accuracy for concurrent post-stroke dementia diagnosis. Further research should establish diagnostic accuracy and clinical utility for post-stroke cognitive syndromes.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 10; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: OCS may be easier to complete with physical, language or visuospatial deficits, but dementia-screening accuracy still needs study. Users should be trained; positive screens warrant comprehensive cognitive assessment and sharing results with the stroke team.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 10; consensus 1

recommendations.text: Consider telephone cognitive screening in post-acute stroke when appropriate; it cannot replace comprehensive assessment. Standard cut-offs identify most important deficits but generate substantial false positives. Accuracy depends on threshold, and the optimal stroke cut-off is unknown.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 11; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: Telephone screening has limitations but can help when in-person assessment is impractical. Video assessment needs further study and interpretation guidance; develop and validate specific remote tools and protocols. Train examiners and follow positive results with comprehensive cognitive assessment, sharing findings with the stroke team.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 11; consensus 1

recommendations.text: In post-stroke cognitive impairment, benefits and risks of cholinesterase inhibitors remain uncertain for cognition, psychological or behavioural symptoms, daily activities and caregiver burden.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 12; recommendation 1

recommendations.section: PICO 12: Cholinesterase inhibitors and mixed pathology
recommendations.text: Any benefit in post-stroke dementia is likely modest and may lack clinical relevance; consider adverse effects. Benefit is minimal in predominantly vascular impairment, but probable mixed neurodegenerative pathology may justify treatment. Prior stroke should not prevent consideration when concomitant Alzheimer's disease or Lewy body dementia is suspected.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 12; consensus 1

recommendations.text: In post-stroke cognitive impairment, memantine's benefits and risks remain uncertain for cognition, psychological or behavioural symptoms, daily activities and caregiver burden.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 13; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: Memantine has, at most, modest benefit in post-stroke dementia and minimal effect in predominantly vascular impairment; weigh adverse effects. Consider it for probable mixed pathology. Stroke should not prevent treatment consideration when concomitant moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease is suspected.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 13; consensus 1

recommendations.text: Benefits and risks of actovegin for post-stroke cognitive impairment remain uncertain; no recommendation can be made.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 14; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: Benefits and risks of cerebrolysin for post-stroke cognitive impairment remain uncertain; no recommendation can be made.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 14; recommendation 2

recommendations.text: Avoid actovegin and cerebrolysin for post-stroke cognitive impairment: possible cognitive gains appear modest, with a risk of serious adverse events. Replicate the single actovegin trial; further studies of either agent need adequate power, longer follow-up, patient-reported outcomes and health-economic evaluation.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 14; consensus 1

recommendations.text: For most cognitive rehabilitation approaches after stroke, robust trials are lacking and benefits and limitations remain uncertain; no evidence-based recommendation can be made.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 15; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: Emerging evidence suggests potential benefit from cognitive rehabilitation, especially compensatory strategies embedded in personally relevant functional tasks. Much of this evidence did not satisfy the PICO inclusion criteria; rigorous trials are needed for definitive practice recommendations.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 15; consensus 1

recommendations.text: The advantages and disadvantages of multi-item tools for predicting cognitive decline or dementia after stroke remain uncertain.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 16; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: Evidence is insufficient to recommend routine tools predicting incident delirium or dementia in stroke care. Studies should follow sound prognostic methods, use adequate samples, handle missing data and validate externally in independent populations. Trials must also test whether using a tool improves clinical care.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 16; consensus 1

recommendations.section: PICO 17: Acute CT and later cognition
recommendations.text: The value of acute brain CT findings for predicting cognitive outcomes more than one year after stroke remains uncertain.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 17; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: Because CT is widely used, its cognitive prognostic value deserves study. Use standardised measurements and validated tools, preferably unselected cohorts with low follow-up loss. Adjust for age, sex and stroke severity to establish added value beyond ordinary clinical information.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 17; consensus 1

recommendations.text: Substantial white matter hyperintensities of presumed vascular origin on acute MRI may help predict cognitive outcomes more than one year after stroke.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 18; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: The prognostic value of acute MRI features other than white matter hyperintensities for cognition more than one year after stroke remains uncertain.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 18; recommendation 2

recommendations.text: White matter lesions have the strongest imaging evidence for later cognitive decline, but incremental value beyond routine clinical factors is unclear. MRI studies should use standardised measures, validated tools, preferably unselected cohorts and low attrition, with adjustment for age, sex and stroke severity.
recommendations.sourceReference: Corrected online supplement 2, recommendation boxes pp.1–19; correction DOI 10.1177/23969873221076951; PICO 18; consensus 1

publicationUpdates.note: The correction restores omitted recommendation boxes in online supplement 2. All 18 PICO questions and their 22 formal/no-recommendation statements plus 18 complete consensus boxes were checked against the corrected supplement.

coverage.scope: All formal recommendations and good-practice/consensus statements
